header_title: Instant Speed: From Secant to Tangent
tagline: An original explainer inspired by Feynman’s lecture topic on motion
question_text: What does speed at a single instant mean?
option_b: (B) A limit of average speed as time shrinks
option_d: (D) The slope of a line segment
correct_answer: The limit of average speed as the time interval shrinks to zero.
audio_script: How can an object have a speed at one exact instant? Track a falling ball between two nearby moments. Its average speed is the change in position divided by the change in time. Now shrink that time gap. The average changes, but approaches a definite value. That limit is the instantaneous speed. On screen, the yellow secant joins two measured positions. As delta t shrinks, it approaches the green tangent at the later point. The tangent’s slope gives the local speed. For motion from rest with constant acceleration, position is one half a t squared, so differentiating gives speed a t. Here a is one meter per second squared. At 2.4 seconds, the speed is 2.4 meters per second. An instant is the limit as the interval shrinks. Average speed describes a stretch of motion; the derivative describes its local rate. That shift in viewpoint is why calculus is so useful in mechanics. The animation makes the limit visible: measure over a gap, then watch the secant settle into the tangent.
